links.title: Mid-Harness: Scaling Actions Between Model and Harness for Terminal Agents

evidence: Abstract: a GPT-5.6 Sol verifier raises TMAX-9B Pass@1 on TerminalBench-Lite from 50.00% (base) to 68.03% with N=8 sampled actions, evidencing exploitable candidate coverage (also Section 4.1, Figure 2).

Section 4.2 / Table 5: zero-shot listwise N=4→8 moves Pass@1 only 49.32%→51.02%, while pairwise reaches 54.76% Pass@1 and 71.43% Pass@3, supporting the claim that verification quality governs the benefit of sampling.

Section 4.3: distillation uses 117,631 frontier-verifier pairwise responses from 244 TMAX-15k tasks with LoRA (Table 4: rank 64, lr 1e-4, 4 H200s), raising Pass@1 54.76%→57.14% and Pass@3 71.43%→75.51%; no confidence interval is reported for the distillation-vs-zero-shot difference.

Appendix C.4 Table 10: task-level bootstrap 95% CIs for base-vs-Mid-Harness; only distilled 9B [+1.36,+12.93] and 27B [+0.34,+9.86] lie above zero, while zero-shot 9B [-0.68,+10.20], 4B, and 27B zero-shot intervals include zero.

Section 6.2 Table 2: transfer across Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21.72→27.34 zero-shot), SWE-bench Verified Mini (46.67→48.67 distilled), FeatureBench-Mini (1.45→7.25 for TMAX-9B), plus Qwen3.5-9B and Nemotron models with Terminus-2; distillation does not improve over zero-shot on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Section 7: acknowledges LLM-as-a-Verifier verifies per-step candidates on Terminal-Bench and Zainullina et al. combine action ranking with trajectory selection, positioning this work as a systematic verification-mechanism study rather than a new method.

Reproducibility statement and Appendices B.2/B.3/B.6: verifier prompts, tournament structure, and training configurations are documented; however, no explicit code or dataset release is stated and the abstract's project page is an unresolved 'link' placeholder.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core agentic-LLM research: test-time compute scaling at the model-harness boundary for terminal agents, directly matching Agents & Tool Use, LLMs, Code & Programming, and Scaling preferences. Rigor is high: systematic comparison of listwise/pointwise/pairwise verification, three model scales, four benchmarks, two harnesses, distillation with disclosed hyperparameters, cost accounting, bootstrap CIs (Appendix C.4), and an offline agreement analysis with held-out tasks. Novelty is moderate because per-step candidate verification already exists (LLM-as-a-Verifier; Zainullina et al., acknowledged in Section 7); the contribution is a careful empirical study rather than a new mechanism. Evidence is generally strong (e.g., 50.00%→68.03% Pass@1 with frontier verification), but several key comparisons lack uncertainty quantification, only distilled 9B/27B CIs exclude zero, zero-shot 9B CI spans [-0.68,10.20], benchmark subsets are small (50 and 23 tasks), and some transfer settings show distillation not beating zero-shot. Reproducibility is aided by full prompts (B.6) and training settings (B.3), but no explicit code/data release is stated and the project-page link is a placeholder.

links.title: Learning Steganography Is Easy, Learning Steganographic Reasoning Is Hard

evidence: Abstract: 'For most tasks, models learn steganographic reasoning only under SFT, while they learn steganographic messaging and encoded reasoning under all three elicitation methods' and 'Even under SFT, steganographic reasoning requires at least twice as much training as messaging'.

Section 3.2: 'Steganographic reasoning is never learned reliably: it plateaus at 69% encoding accuracy at its last evaluation, step 760' while 'messaging within about a hundred RL steps, both reaching near-perfect encoding accuracy'.

Table 2: SFT steps to 95% test encoding accuracy show 2.4x-20x ratios (e.g., Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 500 vs 10,200 steps on sum mod 3) and several non-crossing runs (e.g., Lightning-30B >21,000 steps, final 52%).
Section 3.1/Appendix I: on the knapsack cover, GPT-5.5 reaches 'side-task accuracy at 92% against a 46% no-CoT baseline (chance 50%, p<0.001)', the only model to succeed in-context.
Section 2.3: side tasks chosen by complexity class (modular sum in TC0 vs A5 shell game NC1-complete) so latent computation cannot trivially replace the scratchpad.
Appendix E: monitor validation reports benign inputs at mean suspiciousness 1.1-1.5 (94-99% at/below threshold 3) and conspicuous controls at 8.7-9.9 (0-4% at/below).
Appendix R: error injection shows successful checkpoints follow the corrupted trace beyond the first 3-4 positions (knapsack RL runs 84% and 71%), supporting that the trace is used for computation.

Appendix T: replication of Zolkowski et al. with matched baseline finds 'For word-count it is entirely the task restatement that their encoding instructions leak', with trace decodes at or below chance (0.10-0.40 vs 0.5).
Section 4.3: limitations concede 'our strongest elicitation methods were applied below the frontier' and 'Larger RL runs on frontier models were beyond our budget'.

Introduction: 'We release the code, configurations and results of all experiments, together with the scripts that produce every figure and table' with a GitHub link; Section 2.8 states 'Code, data, and the evaluation harness will be made public upon acceptance' (minor inconsistency).
llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly relevant LLM safety paper on chain-of-thought monitorability and steganographic reasoning, squarely matching LLM (2.5), Reasoning/CoT (2.5), and AI Safety (2.0) preferences. Core contribution is novel and well-posed: a controlled learnability comparison of steganographic reasoning vs. its two components (messaging, encoded reasoning) across ICL, GRPO RL, and SFT, showing steganographic reasoning is far harder to acquire. Rigor is strong: complexity-theoretic side-task design (TC0 vs NC1), monitor validation (Appendix E), per-position breakdowns, error-injection interventions, matched baselines, and paired McNemar/z-tests with Wilson intervals. A thorough replication appendix (T) shows a prior positive result is mostly a prompt leak, which adds credibility. Evidence is quantitative and honestly caveated (trace-usage evidence called 'good, but not conclusive'; mechanism offered only as hypothesis). Generalizability is good across 9+ models and families but RL/SFT were applied below the frontier, as the authors acknowledge (Section 4.3). Reproducibility is aided by verbatim prompts, hyperparameter tables, and a stated code release, though Section 2.8 says 'will be made public upon acceptance' while the introduction claims release.

evidence: Abstract: panel retains a median 93% of the frontier judge's kappa, gives up 2.9 bacc points on average, and runs at a sixty-fourth of the frontier's price
Section 2: stacked logistic regression fitted by 5-fold cross-fitting so every stacked prediction is out-of-fold; 95% paired cluster-bootstrap intervals over B=2000 resamples of clustering units
Section 4: ten members run at $0.039 per 1,000 items vs $2.52 for Sonnet api (~1.55%); break-even between 40,000 and 81,000 evaluated items including $100-$200 calibration labels
Section 4 / Table 8: on LLM-AggreFact-4 the panel reaches 69.5 bacc, drawing level with Granite Guardian 3.3 and inside the agreement band of Bespoke-MiniCheck-7B (71.4) and GPT-4o (70.8)

Appendix B: confirmatory item-level recovery test over 1,998 leader-error items, logistic coefficient +4.67, point-biserial r=+0.41 (p<10^-20); cross-dataset predictor explicitly downgraded to illustrative (rho=+0.47, p=0.24)

Appendix C: admissibility test instance (0.30, 1/2, 0.40) admits MedHallu, WiCE, FActScore; regime call reproduced 85.5% from 50 labelled records; thresholds declared once but 'fixed with the eight results in view, yet not tuned'
Appendix E: leave-one-dataset-out transfer yields zero of four transfer wins with significant transfer cost on MedHallu (+0.111) and RAGTruth (+0.175), bounding deployment generality

Appendix K: multiplicity audit - MedHallu win survives Holm over the four core sets (adjusted p=0.048) but not over all eight (p=0.096); coverage audit shows ~2.1% abstention rate with per-member table
Appendix M: extended limitations name single fixed roster, single frontier judge, English-only suite, binary verdicts only, and kappa readings valid for balanced evaluation

Code and data availability: two GitHub repositories (raim-verdicts, raim-analysis) release the full pipeline, all verdicts including paid api generations, deterministic rebuild with 10^-8 tolerance checks, and content-addressed index
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM methodology paper squarely within the preference set: LLM-as-a-judge, hallucination/faithfulness evaluation, open-weight models, cost-efficient inference. The ensemble-of-judges idea itself is classical (Condorcet, stacked generalization, PoLL), but the paper differentiates with a jointly-fitted cross-fitted stacker that discounts correlated errors, a label-cheap admissibility test, and a priced substitution analysis including calibration labels. Rigor is exceptional and unusually self-critical: paired cluster bootstrap (B=2000), a comparator ladder ordered by labelled information, Holm-corrected key contrasts, surfaced denominator confounds, abstention-encoding and prompt-frame ablations, sub-panel threshold-family checks, and honest reporting of unresolved or negative results (only one clean win over the best single judge; leave-one-dataset-out transfer fails). Evidence is strong within-suite and calibrated against published leaderboards, though cross-dataset mechanism correlations rest on only eight datasets and external comparisons are partly cross-protocol. Generalizability is genuinely bounded by the authors' own limitations: one fixed 10-member roster, a single frontier judge (Claude Sonnet), English-only, binary verdicts, balanced 50/50 tasks, and per-domain calibration. Reproducibility is outstanding: two GitHub repos with full verdicts (including paid API outputs), deterministic analysis rebuild with tolerance checks, and released prompts/decoding settings.

4.3 Table 2: replacing Evaluate-then-Grow with Plan-then-Patch costs 5.3/4.8/4.0 points; collapsing to a single upfront plan totals 14.0/12.6/10.0.

4.3 Table 3: off-chain credit alpha peaks at 0.5 on every benchmark; alpha=0 falls below the GRPO baseline; removing topology credit costs 2.3/1.9/1.7 and removing compliance regularization 1.6/1.0/0.7.

Appendix F Limitations: RL trains only Qwen3-8B with LoRA for 21 update steps; larger-scale/full-fine-tuning persistence not established; closure credit is a structural proxy; compliance-accuracy link is correlational; open-ended report generation out of scope.

4.4 and Appendix D.3 Table 10: same-architecture Plan-then-Patch variant makes 35/27/21% more external tool calls and 35/27/23% more wall-clock time while trailing by 5.3/4.8/4.0 points; Flash-Searcher is cheaper but 8.6/10.6/7.0 points less accurate.

Abstract and 1: code availability claimed at https://github.com/hanwenliu6825/DAGent; prompts listed verbatim in Appendix G, supporting reproducibility.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A deep-research multi-agent paper squarely in scope: LLM backbones, agent orchestration/planning (weight-2.5 preferences), GRPO-based RL with topology-conditioned credit assignment, long-context management, and LLM-as-judge evaluation. Preference relevance is near-maximal. Novelty is moderate: incremental evidence-conditioned DAG growth is a genuine reframing of Plan-then-Patch, and the append-only property enabling topology credit is a clean insight, but graph/DAG credit assignment is a crowded space the paper itself documents (DeepPlanner, OrchDAG, Graph-GRPO, M-GRPO, tree-rollout RL). Rigor is strong: controlled same-backbone comparisons, released FlowSearch implementation as a baseline, two-layer ablations, alpha sensitivity sweep, three training seeds with reported std, and a human agreement study for the judge (aggregate Cohen's kappa 0.95, Appendix C.5). Weaknesses: benchmark N is small (150/103/100 tasks per Appendix C.1 Table 4), training-free rows are single greedy passes without variance, several RL ablation rows are single-seed (acknowledged in 4.3), the GPT-5 comparison borrows numbers from prior reports (Appendix D.1), and no significance testing is provided. Evidence strength is high due to extensive quantitative tables (Tables 1-3, 8-11), per-seed breakdowns (Fig. 7), training dynamics (Fig. 8), behavioral statistics (Fig. 6), and unusually honest hedging (e.g., Appendix D.4 calls the violation-accuracy link correlational). Generalizability is decent (three benchmarks, four vendors plus GPT-5, zero-shot transfer of RL checkpoints) but RL is limited to one 8B backbone with LoRA over 21 update steps and closed-form answers only (Appendix F). Reproducibility is excellent: public code link, full hyperparameter tables (C.2, C.4), baseline caps (C.3), and verbatim prompts (Appendix G).

links.title: Linguistic Loopholes in LLM Unlearning: From a 174-Language Benchmark to Coverage-Aware Unlearning

evidence: Abstract: COVER reduces mean held-out residual access by 7.8–27.3% relative to uniform source selection across three model families and two forget sets.
Section 2: matched source forget protocol with oracle-normalized residual access R and checkpoint stopping thresholds (mean progress ≥0.95, min ≥0.90).
Table 1: benchmark spans 174 language–script pairs, 25 paraphrase types, 103 fine-tuned and 287 unlearned checkpoints over Tiny Aya, Qwen3, and Llama 3.
Table 3: best language subsets improve held-out residual by 14.0–31.4% over uniform; median pairwise Spearman ρ ranges 0.203–0.886 across inventories.
Appendix A.6: LLM judge calibrated against a blind human rater on 192 facts, Cohen's κ=0.64 (fact status) and 0.86 (full leakage).
Table 4c: LORELEI external validation shows smaller gains (+4.60/+2.31 document-beginning for Aya/Qwen) with retention tradeoff (−5.57 ΔchrF++ for Aya).
Section 5: positions contribution against prior multilingual unlearning limited to small high/medium-resource language sets (Choi et al. 2024; Farashah et al. 2026).
Reproducibility statement: project site and GitHub code links provided; full dataset release deferred until after peer review.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core-LLM work squarely matching high-weight preferences (LLMs, AI safety via unlearning/privacy, evaluation/benchmarking, multilingual NLP). Novel formalization of language-budgeted multilingual unlearning and a 174-language benchmark with paraphrase-route analysis substantially extend prior small-language studies (Section 5). Rigor is high: matched-forgetting stopping criterion, oracle-normalized metrics, three model families, three unlearning methods, five training orders, cross-request Spearman correlations, and bootstrap CIs (Section 2, Table 22). Evidence is strong but not airtight: LLM-judge reliance with human calibration κ=0.64 overall (Appendix A.6), overlapping CIs for COVER vs historical best on Llama (Table 4a), small LORELEI gains with measurable retention cost (Table 4c: −5.57 ΔchrF++ for Aya). Generalizability tempered by small 3–4B models and synthetic QA base. Reproducibility good (code/project links, full hyperparameters) but full dataset gated on peer review and benchmark construction depends on proprietary GPT-5.2-chat translations (Appendix B).

links.title: FIGS: Evaluating Multi-Turn Sycophancy Without Penalizing Empathy

evidence: Section 4.3: judge reaches QWK 0.75 (sycophancy) and 0.70 (calibrated validation) on the validation set, above pooled human-human agreement (0.60/0.61), with 0.63/0.66 on a held-out test set (Appendix D, Tables 14-15)

Table 19 (Appendix E): factual prompt lowers sycophancy fail rates for all eight models with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs (e.g., Gemini 3.8 Flash 64.4% to 7.4%) while CV fail rates rise for all eight (Gemini 5.5% to 41.8%); Table 24 gives exact McNemar p-values

Appendix B.3-B.5: replications of SycEval, SYCON, and ELEPHANT; e.g., ELEPHANT validation flags both warranted and sycophantic warm replies (1.00 vs 0.96, Table 3) while the FIGS judge separates them in 48/50 pairs, and ELEPHANT-optimal cold replies fail the CV axis 56.5% of the time (Table 6)

Appendix F.1-F.3: sycophancy rates stable across three user simulators while CV rates rise with simulator strength (Table 26); reruns move fail rates 3-11 points; three independent accuracy prompts reproduce the paternalism trap (Table 27)

Section 7 (Limitations): benchmark is English-only text, synthetic, scored by one judge and one simulator, excludes agentic/multimodal/multilingual sycophancy, and the difficulty filter favors scenarios one evaluated model fails (Appendix C.4)

Section 1 footnote 2, Appendix C.5, D.5, G, and Table 28: code and data on GitHub/HuggingFace, 1,000 judge-labeled transcripts released for judge calibration, verbatim prompts and inference settings documented
llm_evaluation.rationale: LLM sycophancy/safety evaluation benchmark squarely matching high-weight preferences (LLMs, AI safety, red-teaming/evaluation, prompting, alignment). The dual-axis taxonomy separating sycophancy from calibrated validation is a genuine conceptual advance over single-axis or flip-based prior work (SycEval, SYCON, ELEPHANT), and the paper supports the distinction with empirical replications rather than assertion. Rigor is strong: LLM judge validated against human labels exceeding pooled human-human kappa, bootstrap CIs, exact McNemar paired tests, simulator ablation, rerun-variance analysis, and a three-prompt ablation. Limitations are honestly stated: synthetic scenarios with a difficulty filter that biases toward one evaluated model, all scores from a single LLM judge, English-only fixed-length text, and an 'optimal' prompt tuned against the paper's own rubric so its defense result cannot establish generality. Code, 500 frozen scenarios, verbatim prompts, and 1,000 judge-labeled transcripts are released, supporting reproducibility. Score is capped below top tier because findings rest entirely on model-generated conversations and LLM judging, and the headline defense is partially circular.

links.title: PivotOPD: Learning to Recover from Pivotal Mistakes in Multi-Turn Agents

evidence: Abstract: >50% of failed rollouts across three Qwen3 models (8B-235B) contain a pivotal mistake, typically early and recoverable via a few guided turns

Section 2 / Appendix A: counterfactual replay on 72 failed Qwen3-8B trajectories - correcting the pivotal turn raises success from 8.2% [3.8,13.0] to 59.0% [48.3,69.8]; oracle action forced at next two turns reaches 58.3% [47.6,69.1], with 95% bootstrap CIs (4,000 draws)
Table 1: PivotOPD best on all eight per-benchmark averages for Qwen3-1.7B and 8B; ALFWorld avg 73.7 (1.7B) vs strongest baseline 68.0 (OPID), i.e., +5.5%

Table S.4 / Section 5: ablations - random pivotal turns avg 62.6 and recovery-only 64.7 vs PivotOPD 73.7 on ALFWorld, supporting that supervision must land at pivotal turns and that recovery distillation adds beyond prevention (preventive-only 72.5)
Appendix D.6: SWE-Bench Verified transfer with Nemotron-3.5-SFT gives +3.2% resolve rate vs +0.2% for standard OPD, but uses recovery budget K=0 (preventive distillation only)
Table S.1: teacher-oracle agreement - at least one detected pivotal turn within one turn of oracle-labeled turn in 77.8% of failed ALFWorld trajectories on average, vs 28.1-33.6% random baseline

Appendix E.2: replay study over the same 72 oracle-labeled pivotal mistakes - PivotOPD final recovery rate 72.7% vs 8.3% (base), 20.3% (standard OPD), 45.8% (preventive only); PivotOPD improves 60 of 72 mistakes and worsens none

Appendix G: limitations - K>1 requires exactly replayable environments, wrong teacher actions become wrong targets, and K and w_rec must be swept per benchmark; diagnosis relies on ALFWorld's symbolic oracle which other benchmarks lack
Appendix E.1 / Table S.5: training overhead quantified (e.g., K=1 adds ~12.4% over GRPO per step on ALFWorld; K=2 adds ~94.2%), and no inference-time cost since the teacher is dropped at test time
Tables S.2/S.3 and Section D.4: full hyperparameters and prompt templates provided, but no explicit code or data release statement appears in the document
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM-agent training methodology: on-policy distillation plus group-based RL (PPO) for Qwen3/Nemotron LLMs on multi-turn agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, Search-based QA, SWE-Bench Verified), squarely matching high-weight preferences (LLMs, agents, reasoning, RL, code). Novelty is solid but incremental over identified prior work: PivotRL/OPID already concentrate training on pivotal/skill turns (Appendix F), OPSD provides privileged self-teachers; the genuinely new elements are teacher-detected pivot detection without an oracle and forward-KL recovery distillation at post-mistake states (Sections 3.2-3.4). Rigor is strong: 13 baselines under shared data/teacher/tuning budget (Section 4.1, D.3), three seeds, oracle-based counterfactual diagnosis with bootstrap CIs (Appendix A), matched-budget controls (random turns, hints w/o gold actions, reverse-KL recovery, preventive/recovery-only) in Tables 2/S.4, teacher-oracle agreement quantified (Table S.1), leakage control (Appendix B), and propositions with proofs (Appendix C). Evidence is credible but with caveats: main tables report three-seed means without variance; the SWE-Bench transfer uses K=0 (preventive only, Appendix D.6), so the headline recovery mechanism is untested there; margins shrink to +1.8% at 8B. Generalizability is supported across two model families and four benchmarks but limited by the need for exactly replayable environments, teacher reliability, and per-benchmark sweeps of K and w_rec (Appendix G). Reproducibility is decent (hyperparameters Tables S.2/S.3, prompts in D.4, Algorithm 1) but no explicit code/data release is stated.

links.title: Unlearnable, or Unmeasured? On the Reliability of Difficulty Labels in RLVR

evidence: Section 3.2: unlearnable cohort reward slope is +0.0422 [+0.0259,+0.0590] per 100 optimizer steps vs +0.1119 for learnable, establishing slow-learning rather than literal non-learning.
Section 3.3: holding 292 sub-threshold candidates fixed, the published five-seed rule returns 74 prompts vs 228 under an alternative aggregation; individual seeds span 145-150 (mean 147.8).

Section 3.4/Appendix B.3: two prospectively frozen predictions (N=40: predicted 0.8131, measured 0.8450; N=64: predicted 0.8397, measured 0.8742) both fall inside pre-registered intervals; 0.90 agreement projects 242 rollouts.

Section 3.5/Appendix C.2: matching correct-rollout count reduces the easy-to-D_u gradient-similarity ratio from 2.327x to 1.539x [1.26,1.88], with attrition to 28 of 71 D_u prompts explicitly flagged as a selection effect.
Appendix E: full 47-constant configuration audit (30 match, 17 differ), single RTX 3090 Ti compute disclosure, and code/rollout artifact release promised 'upon acceptance'.

Section 3.6/Appendix D.2: two difficulty constructions removing 5.0% vs 27.6% of usable training signal yield models differing by less than one held-out accuracy point, with the authors correctly noting registered sensitivity cannot support an equivalence claim.
llm_evaluation.rationale: In-scope core LLM post-training research: a measurement/reproducibility audit of difficulty labels in RLVR (GRPO on Qwen2.5-0.5B, MATH), directly engaging RL, reasoning, and LLM evaluation preferences. Methodologically strong: bootstrap CIs, equal-cost budget allocation controls, generation-length confound checks, matched-sample gradient reanalysis with explicit selection-effect caveats, and two prospectively frozen predictions that validated. Novelty is solid but it is a reanalysis rather than a new method or mechanism; the transferable contribution is the sampling-budget procedure, not the specific numbers, which limits generalizability beyond one dataset/model scale. Reproducibility is well supported by a 47-constant configuration audit and planned artifact release, though release is contingent on acceptance and the replication is not byte-for-byte identical (1,024 vs 5,120 token cap).

evidence: Abstract: claims 85.04% average improvement over SOTA on a 300 multi-patch CVE benchmark and public release of https://patch-relation.com
Section II-A: taxonomy derived from 1,050 multi-patch CVE entries plus interviews with 20 developers with 7+ years experience, yielding six relationship types

Section IV-C: benchmark of 300 CVEs (2-7 patches each, 694 patches, 473 relationship instances) across 213 repositories spanning 2009-2024, Cohen's Kappa 87.98% with third-expert disagreement resolution

Section VII: threats to validity address annotator subjectivity, LLM data-leakage risk (labels newly created; DS-only underperforms COMPASS), and limited ecosystem coverage

llm_evaluation.rationale: LLM-centric software engineering paper squarely within preference space: the method's core is structured LLM prompting (chain-of-thought intuition, hierarchy-guided prompts, one-shot demonstrations, validation phase) applied to a new task—predicting relationships among multiple patches for the same CVE. Rigor is solid: 300-CVE benchmark disjoint from taxonomy set, 473 instances with Cohen's Kappa 87.98%, four LLM backbones compared, six fine-tuned pre-trained-model baselines with 10-fold CV, an LLM-only control isolating pipeline gains, and ablations of one-shot prompting and supporting phases; the headline 85.04% average relative F1 improvement is internally consistent with Table II values. Weaknesses: no statistical significance testing, single-LLM DS-only control, taxonomy explicitly non-exhaustive, and scope limited to vulnerability patches without industrial validation. Reproducibility claims are concrete (public repository with prompts/code/data, online website patch-relation.com), though link liveness is unverifiable from the text.

links.title: From Spectra to Joint Schedules in LLM Pre-training: 3+3(+2) Scaling-Law Regimes

evidence: Abstract: 'Controlled nanoGPT experiments show that (1) learning-rate and batch-size schedules with matched B/eta paths are nearly equivalent in intrinsic time, (2) a forcing-memory surrogate accurately predicts loss across schedules'; code at github.com/yichenblue/spectra-to-schedules-in-pretraining
Theorem 3.1 (Sec. 3): 'nu_W^F((0,x]) prop x^{q_F} iff F_{W,>0}(t) prop T^{-q_F}' — cumulative weighted spectral mass, not coordinatewise power laws, determines component power laws

Theorem 5.1 (Sec. 5): q_N(vartheta) piecewise formula and preserve/change/destroy classification comparing noise exponent to clean exponent q_0, with a 'memory ceiling' beyond which late-stage noise reduction cannot improve decay
Sec. 5.4 / Fig. 6: independently fitted q_K = 1.017 (OpenWebText), 0.952 (FineWeb), 0.995 (peS2o V2), each fitted only on 8-1-1 and transferred to WSD 'without refitting'

Appendix F.1: 30M nanoGPT, plain SGD, B=8, eleven ratio paths vartheta in {0,...,2} stopped at matched intrinsic time; authors state 'This experiment tests these predictions only qualitatively. It uses one seed... and does not independently estimate q_K'

Appendix F.2: 300M nanoGPT, 6.5B OpenWebText tokens (5.2B prefix + 1.3B tail); plain-SGD trajectories 'nearly coincide' under B/eta in intrinsic time, Muon under B/eta^2 (empirically calibrated, 'not identified with the plain-SGD ratio')
Remark A.5 and Assumption A1: 'the simultaneous width–time uniformity used above is assumed' and empirical-to-DE transfer is assumed — key bridging conditions not proved
Appendix F.3 (unrestricted fit): all seven parameters free gives q_K=0.989, q_F=0.291; authors caution this 'does not independently identify an asymptotic memory exponent'
llm_evaluation.rationale: A theory-first paper on LLM pre-training scaling laws and joint learning-rate/batch-size schedules, squarely matching the LLM (2.5) and Scaling & Efficiency (1.3) preferences plus Training & Optimization. It proves componentwise spectral iff-criteria for power-law forcing/memory (Theorems 3.1/A.4), a sharp preserve-change-destroy schedule classification (Theorem 5.1, Appendix D), and phase-wise compute-optimal rates (Corollary 5.2, Table 1), then bridges to LLMs via a 7-parameter forcing-memory surrogate tested on nanoGPT across OpenWebText/FineWeb/peS2o with q_K=1.017/0.952/0.995 (Sec. 5.4, Appendix F.3). Novelty is solid but partly derivative of Paquette et al. (2024) 4+3 regimes and Li et al. (2025) FSL; the extension adds label noise, joint schedules, and a new 3+3(+2) propagation taxonomy. Rigor is high: extensive proved theorems with explicit stability/spectral-window assumptions, though key uniformity assumptions (Remark A.5, Assumption A1, C.19) are assumed rather than proved. LLM evidence is meaningful but limited: plain-SGD nanoGPT at 30M-300M, one seed in the ratio-path test (Appendix F.1 admits it is qualitative), and proxy-to-LLM validity is empirical, not proved. Code is released and protocols are detailed, aiding reproducibility. Generalizability beyond power-law spectra, SGD, and small-scale models is qualified by the authors themselves (Muon uses different coordinates, Appendix F.2).

Novelty is solid but incremental: it reframes post-rollout consolidation as relational selection (graph message passing over shared evidence across rollouts) rather than voting or generative aggregation, differing from independent verifiers and AggAgent-style LLM aggregation. links.title: DoGBench: Can Agents Meet Expert Standards for User-Facing Documentation?

evidence: Abstract: 'The benchmark contains 292 items from open source projects... The highest-scoring agent reached 47.3 out of 100 on the 117-item held-out split' with failure rates (45.5% task-completion gaps, 36.6% technical inaccuracies) from a 1,267-patch audit.

Section 4.4 (Human validation): 'mean priority-weighted recall against maintainer criteria is 0.892' and 'the scoring model agrees with the post-adjudication human reference on 310 criteria (93.9%)'; the paper notes this is 'not blinded agreement between two humans'.

Section 3.2 (Contamination controls): 'agents work in fresh Docker containers with identity-masked repositories and no network access'; earlier pilot found '31% of runs retrieved the source pull request despite identity masking'.

Section 6.3 (Ablations): source-event-date ablation reports 'every repository-clustered interval includes zero, so the comparison provides no statistically conclusive evidence of a cutoff effect'; documentation-scale ablation CI [−2.81, +0.69] includes zero.

Section 9.3 (Limitations): 'Some abstention labels... rely only on the absence of a related documentation change within a 90-day audit window', acknowledging asymmetric label noise; Section 9.4 admits single-run evaluation with no pass@k or run-to-run variance.

Appendix B.2: generated rubrics cover '90.9% of 242 maintainer-validated criteria', pooled Spearman 0.755 and Krippendorff alpha 0.805 between generated and maintainer rubric scores; Section 8.4 concedes scaffolding interventions were 'explored informally but did not systematically compare' against a baseline.
Section 9 Disclosure: 'Two authors are affiliated with Promptless, a company that builds documentation agents' — a disclosed potential conflict of interest.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A well-executed agentic benchmark paper squarely in high-weight preference areas: coding agents, tool use, LLM evaluation, and software documentation. Novelty is solid—the abstention/patch decision and user-facing documentation focus are claimed as firsts and are differentiated from code-facing doc benchmarks (CoDocBench, CodeWikiBench, SWD-Bench)—though rubric-based LLM-judge scoring of open-ended edits is an established pattern (RubricBench, Mei et al.). Rigor is strong: maintainer validation of rubrics (0.892 priority-weighted recall on 21 items; 93.9% scorer agreement on 330 criteria), contamination controls (sealed Docker, identity masking, cutoff and footprint ablations), and an unusually candid limitations section (single-run design, asymmetric abstention labels from a 90-day window, LLM-judge dependence, disclosed vendor affiliation). Evidence is quantitative with clustered bootstrap CIs and a 1,267-submission failure audit, but validation subsets are small, the P0 60-point cap is policy rather than estimated, and mechanistic explanations (coarse rewards, stopping rules) are speculative links to prior work. Generalizability is decent across OSS ecosystems but limited to English docs and incremental maintenance. Reproducibility is aided by released harness/dev split and a public site, yet private held-out rubrics and proprietary judge models constrain exact replication.

Novelty is solid but builds on Liars' Bench, Schouten et al., and Sturgeon et al., with the on-policy dataset being the clearest new asset. evidence: Section 3.1-3.2: Rheon models each agent response as an O(n) semantic spin plus a binary factual spin; Eraclitus-4.7M is generated from 432 configurations (6 prompts x 12 sizes x 6 temperatures) across a 1D ring/2D torus/3D torus/mean-field ladder, totalling 4,767,840 LLM calls with Qwen3-14B (4-bit) as the frozen backbone.

Appendix C, Table 8: the LLM-as-a-judge (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) is validated against two blind human annotators on 1,063 stratified responses; pooled kappa=0.760/0.791 and 98.58% raw agreement on Prompts 2-6, while Prompt 1 shows systematic label inversion (34% agreement, kappa=0.025), leading to its principled exclusion.

Section 4.1 / Figure 4: the hallucination-minimising temperature depends on coupling — 2D at N_a=256 repairs at T=0.1 (Delta rho=-0.98) and 3D at N_a=216 (-1.00), whereas mean-field repairs best at T*~1.0 (-0.81) with near-zero repair at cold settings (-0.20 at T=0.1).

Table 2 / Section 5 Insight 4: Pearson correlation between semantic cohesion and factual accuracy rises from mean +0.09 (t=0) to +0.15 (t=10) with a maximum of +0.36 and several non-significant configurations, supporting the claim that unanimity never certifies correctness.

Appendix E, Tables 9-10: the geometry ladder 1D<2D<3D<MF in final cohesion holds under all four sentence encoders (MF c_bar ~0.92 in every case), and per-configuration cohesion rankings are encoder-invariant (Spearman 0.899-0.962).

Section 5 'Scope and limitations': homogeneous population (one frozen model, one prompt per run, no personas or adversaries) on regular geometries within a ten-sweep horizon; Appendix A.6 specifies a 2,160-file Parquet layout (~39 GB) with full row schema, while Section 6 states code and corpus 'will be made publicly available', i.e., release is promised not verified.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core-scope LLM research: multi-agent populations of interacting LLMs, consensus/hallucination dynamics, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. The physics-inspired Rheon framework (O(n) semantic spins + Ising factual spins, Glauber dynamics, geometry ladder, temperature as thermal disorder) is a genuinely novel analytical lens on agent consensus, backed by a large 4.7M-response released corpus. Rigor is strong: fixed 100-token outputs, top_p=1 so temperature is the only noise channel, embedding whitening, finite-size-floor-corrected cohesion, 5 independent trials, human validation of the judge including transparent documentation of its Prompt-1 label inversion, and 4-encoder robustness checks. Evidence is broad but partially thin: pivotal temperature-geometry interaction claims (e.g., cold optimum only under local coupling with large populations) rest mainly on one prompt and R=5 trials with very large dispersion (rho=0.50±0.58 in MF), and cohesion-accuracy correlations are weak (max r=+0.36, many non-significant). Generalizability is limited by a single frozen Qwen3-14B backbone, six FreshQA prompts, homogeneous agents, and a 10-sweep horizon, all acknowledged by the authors. Reproducibility is high on paper (seeds derived from configuration, full schema, judge template, Algorithm 1, ~39 GB artifact) but release is promised rather than confirmed.

Appendix A.2: 'Because this configuration changes the continuation length and the prefix-cut spacing together, the comparison does not isolate either change'
Appendix B: 'The per-step Pearson correlation is r=0.874' between decoding FLOPs and GPU hours; mean-based FLOPs estimates fall 4.01-5.51% below exact costs
Appendix A.3: 'AC2 and GRPO plateau at roughly the same score' for best-of-16

Footnote: 'Code available at https://github.com/WhenWen/AC2'; Table 4 lists full hyperparameters including τ_global=0.20, τ_local=0.18, chunk length b=10,000
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core on-topic LLM research: a new RLVR algorithm (Actor-Critic with Action Chunking) for training Qwen3-4B on mathematical proof reasoning, directly touching LLM (2.5), Reasoning/CoT (2.5), RL (1.5), Training & Optimization (1.5), and Scaling & Efficiency (1.5) preferences. Novelty is solid but not breakthrough: the paper itself concedes its three ingredients (privileged critic, readiness gating, chunking) each have precedent (Section 5), with the claimed novelty being the first λ=0 GAE advantage estimator that removes terminal-reward dependence in LLM RLVR (Section 5: 'to our knowledge AC2 is the first method to date to use λ=0'). Rigor is strong: tuned GRPO baseline (Appendix A.1), a Prefix GRPO control isolating replay state distribution, careful FLOPs accounting with GPU-hour correlation r=0.874 (Appendix B), and many ablations. Evidence is weakened by single runs with no seeds/error bars, LLM-judge rewards (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Section 4) with no reported judge validation, moderate advantage correlation of 0.388 (Section 4.4), a confounded chunk-size ablation (Appendix A.2 admits it 'does not isolate either change'), and honest reporting that best-of-16 scores plateau equally for AC2 and GRPO (Appendix A.3). Generalizability is limited: one model, one domain (Olympiad proofs), and the authors acknowledge local readiness requires epoching data, which 'is not realistic' in single-epoch regimes (Section 6). Reproducibility is high: code URL, full hyperparameter table (Table 4), verbatim critic prompts, and exact FLOPs formulas.

links.title: Semifactual Credit-Augmented Policy Optimization

evidence: Abstract: SCAPO improves AIME 2024–2026 accuracy over GRPO by 5.63 and 4.17 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base; verified against Table 1 (27.71 vs 22.08; 11.88 vs 7.71).

Section 2 / Figure 3 / Appendix C.3 Table 5: d-filtered decoding raises frozen Qwen3-4B-Base accuracy from 15.8% to 30.0% on a 1,000-question DAPO-Math-17K panel (202 incorrect-to-correct vs 60 correct-to-incorrect transitions).

Section 3.2–3.4: Fixed-response teacher-forced probing (Eq. 5–6), group-relative standardized stability (Eq. 7–8), and detached negative-only advantage augmentation Ã = A + λ·sg(u⁻) (Eq. 9) with schedule λ=λ0 for n≤N0 (Eq. 11).

Section 4.3 Table 2: Ablations on Qwen3-1.7B-Base show negative-only semifactual credit (avg 17.65) beats random shuffle (13.65), counterfactual answer-changing perturbations (11.68), all-sign (15.65), and positive-only (14.05).
Section 4.4 / Figure 5: semifactual probing and credit construction account for only 1.8% of measured training runtime in the 4B experiment.
Appendix A Limitations: experiments limited to dense Qwen3 1.7B/4B on DAPO-Math-17K; larger scales, MoE/hybrid architectures, and broader domains remain untested.

Reproducibility Statement + Appendix E (Table 6, Table 7, Table 3): code released at github.com/DtYXs/SCAPO on EasyR1, full hyperparameters, generation prompts, and per-benchmark sample counts provided.

Appendix D: Lemma D.1 bounds the auxiliary gradient perturbation by λH with H=RB/2; Theorem D.2 shows the augmentation term in the stationarity bound decays as N0/T after the finite augmentation phase.

Table 8: yearly AIME/AMC/HMMT/NoOp/ThinkBench breakdowns corroborate aggregate claims; SCAPO best on 6/8 in-distribution metrics at 4B (Minerva and OlympiadBench won by FIPO) and 8/8 at 1.7B, matching the abstract's 'most benchmarks' phrasing.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM reasoning/RLVR methodology paper, squarely in scope. SCAPO augments GRPO token-level advantages with a detached, negative-only stability signal derived from teacher-forced probability drift under answer-preserving semifactual prompt perturbations; the diagnostic finding that drift-filtered decoding lifts frozen Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.8% to 30.0% without weight updates is a genuinely interesting, novel contribution distinct from span-masking (CF-GRPO) and future-KL (FIPO) credit methods. Rigor is solid: five matched baselines sharing data/reward/protocol, ablations on credit source (random shuffle, counterfactual) and sign, a stochastic-gradient perturbation bound (Appendix D), and an efficiency analysis (1.8% runtime overhead). Evidence is extensive and internally consistent (AIME 27.71 vs 22.08 at 4B; 11.88 vs 7.71 at 1.7B; OOD wins on NoOp/ThinkBench/GPQA at both scales), but drawn from single runs without variance or significance reporting, and the λ0/N0 augmentation schedule risks eval-tuned hyperparameters. Generalizability is limited by the paper's own admission (Appendix A) to dense Qwen3 1.7B/4B on DAPO-Math-17K math domain; GPQA transfer is suggestive but narrow. Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameters (Table 6), exact perturbation prompts (Table 3), evaluation counts (Table 7), and released code on EasyR1.

evidence: Abstract: 'FAME achieves AUROCs of 76.2%-96.7% across false-memory settings, and outperforms the best baseline by 3.4%-23.3% across realistic benchmarks, spanning math reasoning (GSM-Symbolic), code generation (GitChameleon), and complex reasoning (BigBench-Hard)'
Sec. 3.1: structural causal model of belief update with 3-step counterfactual framework (Pearl 2009); Prop. 1 and Thms. 1-3 stated with proofs in App. B.1-B.4

Sec. 5.1: 'We leverage Llama-3B in the experiments. We obtain the hidden states at the 14th layer'; AUROC metric; five baselines including cloud distance, task vector, input similarity, logit confidence
Table 1 (Sec. 5.2): FAME 0.922/0.966/0.869/0.762 across spurious keeping/removal, environment shift, knowledge conflict vs. best baseline 0.782/0.751/0.788/0.652
Fig. 4 (Sec. 5.2): 'overlapping answer confidence distributions between correct and false memory answers' demonstrating answer-only monitoring fails
Table 2 (Sec. 6): realistic benchmarks, FAME best in all six settings, e.g., 0.786/0.790/0.860 (GSM), 0.716 (Git), 0.815/0.861 (BBH)
App. D.2 (Table 3): ablations with 10 random subsamples show removing expectation drops AUROC to 0.445-0.559 and random-direction g_O to 0.464-0.503
App. D.4 (Tables 5-7): FAME outperforms baselines on Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-3B with per-model layer sweeps (16th/14th/36th layers)
App. C.2: readout direction g_O built from J=50/40/20 held-out query pairs per template; ground-truth labels 'used solely for evaluation'
Sec. 7: limitation - 'FAME requires access to agent hidden states and counterfactual queries'; Sec. 6.1: 'we curate and release a suite of templates' (40 GSM, 18 Git, 11 BBH)
llm_evaluation.rationale: Strongly on-topic for the curator's preferences: an LLM-agent memory evaluation framework (Agents 2.5x, LLMs 2.5x, Reasoning 2.5x, Interpretability 1.8x, RAG/knowledge-conflict 1.8x) spanning math reasoning, code generation, and complex reasoning benchmarks. FAME formalizes 'false memory' via an SCM, proves counterfactual/concept-drift identifiability (Props/Thms 1-3 with proofs in App. B), and realizes it training-free from residual-stream hidden states with admissible-region boundaries. Novelty is solid though it assembles known ingredients (task/function vectors, ICL-as-concept, Mahalanobis cloud distance, ETT); the answer-free detection of belief failures invisible in answer confidence distributions (Fig. 4) is a genuinely interesting contribution. Rigor is good: controlled taxonomy settings (Sec. 5), realistic benchmarks (Sec. 6, Tab. 2), ablations (App. D.2: random-direction and expectation-swap controls collapse to ~0.45-0.55 AUROC), robustness checks (App. D.3), and cross-LLM generalization (App. D.4, Llama-8B/Mistral-7B/Qwen2.5-3B with layer sweeps). Weaknesses: main experiments use only a 3B model; template pools are small (40/18/11); threshold selection and readout-direction construction rely on curated held-out queries (App. C.2, Eq. 36); white-box hidden-state access limits applicability (acknowledged in Sec. 7); ground truths are author-constructed. Evidence is quantitative and internally consistent (Tab. 1 AUROCs 0.762-0.966 match abstract claims), but effect sizes come from modest-scale curated settings. Reproducibility is moderate: counterfactual templates are released, Alg. 1 and hyperparameters are specified, but no explicit code release for the framework itself.

links.title: Revisiting On-policy Adversarial Black-Box Distillation: Calibrating Groupwise Reward Geometry for Effective Advantage Construction

evidence: Abstract: proposes GRGC, a two-stage framework (Gaussian groupwise OT calibration + policy-side group power modulation), and states code is available at https://github.com/2018cx/GRGC

Section 3.2/Appendix C, Proposition 1: Jensen's inequality shows the BT critic loss is uniquely minimized at zero within-group student dispersion on fixed-mean slices, diagnosing the critic-to-advantage mismatch
Section 4.1: teachers are API-based GPT-5 and Doubao-Seed-2.0; students are Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B/3B and Llama-3.2-Instruct 1B/3B; 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs; group size N=8, lambda_OT=0.01, gamma=1.5
Table 2: on LMSYS with GPT-5 teacher, GRGC reaches 50.19 score / 45.3% win vs GAD 48.44 / 25.1% for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
Table 5: ablation isolating CGC and PGM; CGC alone at 1 epoch (47.52) is below GAD (48.44) for Qwen2.5-3B, which the text in Section 4.2 explicitly discusses
Table 8: measured training overhead of 0.11% (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and 0.06% (Qwen2.5-3B) per step
Appendix G.10, Tables 20-21: five-seed judge evaluation with 95% CIs (e.g., GRGC mean 50.19, std 0.03) showing gains exceed judge-sampling variability
Tables 17-19 (Appendix G.7-G.9): rule-based IFEval, Math500 (49.6% vs GAD 44.0%), Minerva Math and Gaokao-MathQA gains provide judge-free corroboration
Appendix J: acknowledges the method inherits GAD's cost, being slower than SeqKD, a real tradeoff
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM methodology work: black-box distillation from frontier API teachers (GPT-5-Chat, Doubao-Seed-2.0) into small open students via GAD-style adversarial critics and GRPO, directly hitting the LLM, RLHF/alignment, and training preferences. The paper contributes a genuine diagnosis (Proposition 1: the Bradley-Terry critic objective, via Jensen's inequality, uniquely favors collapsed within-group student reward dispersion at fixed mean, which harms GRPO advantage construction) and a two-part fix (Gaussian groupwise OT calibration on the critic; signed-power reward modulation before advantage computation). Novelty is moderate: OT regularization and reward shaping are standard tools, the setting is an increment on GAD, and the theory (Jensen, Cauchy-Schwarz, Lipschitz bounds in Appendix C) is elementary though correct and well-integrated. Rigor is strong: component ablations (Table 5), alternatives for both calibration prior (Table 6) and transform (Table 7), hyperparameter sensitivity (Tables 12-13), mechanism diagnostics (Tables 1, 9, 10), honest discussion that CGC alone underperforms GAD at 1 epoch, complexity analysis (Appendix H), and an explicit limitations section (Appendix J). Evidence is broad and consistent: 2 teachers x 4 students x 2 training sets, four eval sets, three judges (Qwen2.5-72B, GPT-OSS-120B, humans), judge-free IFEval/Math500/Minerva/Gaokao results (Tables 17-19), and multi-seed CIs (Tables 20-21). Weaknesses: reliance on LLM-as-judge whose reference is generated by the same judge family (mitigated but not eliminated), students capped at 1-3B, theory offers sufficiency-type guarantees only, and effect sizes on some OOD sets are modest. Reproducibility is good: code link, pseudocode (Appendix E), full hyperparameters and eval prompts, though teachers require paid API access.

evidence: Abstract: 'At −70% compression, LSP brings Llama-2-7B to 10.9 WikiText-2 perplexity and 42.2% mean zero-shot accuracy, versus 13.3 and 36.0% for the strongest baseline'
Table 1 / Section 3.1: one of the two LSP variants attains the lowest perplexity in all 12 model–ratio settings, with the margin growing with compression ratio
Section 2.1: learnable orthogonal projector P = I − UU^T optimized end-to-end with frozen weights using unconstrained V with fused QR orthonormalization

Appendix A.7 (Limitations): 'the measured-KL allocation is a local surrogate... no global-optimality guarantee'; Appendix B quantifies joint KL exceeding summed isolated costs by 2.1–4.3× on Llama-2-7B and 1.5–14× on ViT
Table 6 (Appendix B): three-seed mean ± standard deviation for all main LSP results, e.g. Llama-2-7B −70% LSP 10.94 ± 0.12 perplexity

Section 3.2 / Table 3: matched-size single (CIFAR-100 only) vs diverse calibration pools isolate calibration-shift robustness; LSP shows largest transfer gain (+6.6 to +7.1 points) from pool composition

Section 3.3 / Table 5: measured CUDA-graph decode throughput on GH200 (LSP 221 tok/s vs 191 for SVD-LLM at −70%); Appendix E notes latent-cache memory and context capacity are analytic estimates from factor widths

Appendix B: exhaustive hyperparameters, baseline tuning sweeps, identical calibration budgets across methods, held-out validation selection; however, no public code release for LSP itself is stated in the document
llm_evaluation.rationale: A methodological paper on low-rank compression of pretrained transformers (LSP) that learns which weight subspace to remove end-to-end against a global objective (KL distillation or task loss) with frozen weights. It squarely targets LLM efficiency (Llama-2-7B, Qwen3-4B, OPT) plus a secondary ViT experiment, matching LLM and efficiency-related preferences but not the highest-weight topics (agents, reasoning, Japanese LLM). The core idea—replacing local closed-form subspace selection (activation energy, layer-wise reconstruction, curvature surrogates) with globally learned orthogonal projectors, tied groups, whitened initialization, and measured-KL rank allocation—is a genuine advance, though the paper itself situates it as bringing the known local-to-global shift in structured pruning into low-rank compression, tempering novelty. Rigor is high: a proven proposition, a complete algorithm, ablations of initialization/tying/allocation, three-seed variance, matched calibration budgets, and swept baselines. Evidence is strong with consistent quantitative tables and measured throughput; caveats include analytic (not measured) latent-cache memory figures and domain specialization when calibrating on the WikiText-2 training split. The limitations section candidly admits the allocation surrogate is additive and non-optimal (joint KL exceeds summed isolated costs by 2.1–4.3× on Llama-2-7B). Generalizability is demonstrated across decoder LLMs with different attention routing and a ViT, but is confined to transformer linear layers; no explicit public code release for LSP is stated despite exhaustive implementation detail.

llm_evaluation.rationale: Core agentic-LLM research: evolving an agent harness (tools, context, skills, memory, workflows) around a fixed LLM backbone, matching Agents & Tool Use (2.5), LLMs (2.5), memory/context, and coding-agent preferences; squarely in scope, not a pure domain application. links.title: Synthetic Pre-pretraining Survives Scale, but Not as a Grammatical Prior

evidence: Abstract/Section 1: claims first systematic PPT study spanning five PPT tasks, four PT mixtures, 500M-7B parameters, and up to 100B tokens; 'saving at least 21B PT tokens at the 3B scale'

Section 5.1/Figure 2: k-Shuffle Dyck improves downstream average in 9 of 12 scale-mixture pairs (mean gain 1.6 among them); Control stays within -0.2 to +0.4 of PT-Only, isolating the synthetic-data effect

Section 6/Table 3b and Appendix Table 14: formal and non-formal tasks (Dyck +1.3, MP-Struct +0.9, NCA +1.2) all help while Set, lacking positional retrieval, degrades by -7.2, supporting the retrieval hypothesis
Section 6/Table 4 and Table 15: on Marin 3B, PPT reaches 62.3 average after 63B tokens vs PT-Only 62.0 after 84B; gains persist at 7B (positive at every budget up to 75.5B)
Footnote 3: 'Compute constraints limit 7B evaluations to the Marin mixture (up to 75.5B PT tokens) and k-Shuffle Dyck' - a scope limitation
Appendix B.2: three-seed replication on Marin 3B shows downstream gain varies by only 0.2 points (seed means +1.9/+1.9/+1.7) and BLiMP sign instability (+0.9 to -0.3) reproduces

Reproducibility Statement: code, preprocessing and training guides at github.com/gucci-j/verify-ppt-at-scale; checkpoints and datasets on Hugging Face Hub (verify-ppt); Appendix A.2 gives full hyperparameters, software versions, and GPU-hours (PPT = 4.74% of wall-clock)
Section 6: authors concede 'We leave a direct ablation of OLMo3, and the property responsible for this gap, for future work'
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM pre-training science: a well-designed scale study showing synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) benefits persist from 500M to 7B and up to 100B tokens, while refuting the grammatical-prior explanation in favor of a long-range retrieval mechanism. Relevance is solid but not maximal: it targets the LLM/training/scaling/synthetic-data clusters rather than the highest-weighted agent, reasoning, or Japanese-LLM preferences, and is English-only. Novelty is good - first systematic PPT evaluation at scale plus a credible overturning of prior attribution (Hu et al. 2025) - though the mechanism claim remains task-level inference rather than mechanistic analysis. Rigor is strong: controlled PT-Only and text-warm-up Control baselines (Section 4.2), checkpoint averaging with SDs and a 'stable' criterion, averaging-window sweeps (Table 10), and 3-seed replication on the key 3B Marin config (Appendix B.2, gain varies only 0.2 points). Evidence is extensive and quantified (Tables 2-4, 14-16): downstream gains in 9/12 scale-mixture pairs, verbatim NLL reduced in all 12 pairs (stable in 7) vs BLiMP stable in 1/12, 13x math-share increase leaves gain unchanged while removing web text collapses it to +0.2 (Table 3a), and 100B-token runs show PPT reaching PT-Only's 84B-token quality. Weaknesses: single runs for most grid cells, 7B limited to one mixture and one PPT task (footnote 3), the OLMo3 anomaly is left unexplained, and no formal significance testing. Generalizability is broad by design but constrained by the SmolLM3 architecture and English benchmarks. Reproducibility is excellent with full hyperparameters, compute costs, and public code/checkpoints/datasets.

llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM post-training methodology: value-model-free RLVR (GRPO/SPO) with a new token-level credit assignment signal (proximal entropy), evaluated on mathematical reasoning and held-out code. Novelty is moderate: the method is an incremental but well-motivated refinement of entropy-based advantage shaping (80/20, Entropy Adv., GTPO, ARES), with the local-vs-global reference frame and confounder analysis (prompt difficulty, positional trend) as the main conceptual contribution plus a simple invariance proof. links.title: Safety of Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems

evidence: Abstract: reward-guided attack raises mean harmful-compliance from 27.9 (benignly trained links) to 76.9 across three topologies and four safety benchmarks.
Section 3, Table 1: benign latent link training raises aggregate ASR from 4.4→31.1 (2-agent), 3.2→31.7 (sequential), 12.5→20.8 (mixture) while all agent parameters remain frozen.

Section 3, Figure 2: first-token refusal probability drops from 0.82/0.84 (receiver alone/text) to 0.29 with trained link; forcing 'Sorry' prefix lowers compliance 31.1→1.6, supporting the shallow-alignment interpretation.
Section 4.1, Table 2: supervised optimization raises aggregate compliance 27.9→75.6 but cuts MATH500 from 67.2%→30.7%; 10% data poisoning alone raises it to 58.2.
Section 5.2, Table 4: reward-guided repair reduces aggregate harmful compliance from 70.3 to 4.8 averaged over nine attack-topology pairs, e.g., mixture RL attack 95.9→2.5.
Appendix B.3: the attack judge J_ψ is implemented with the StrongREJECT judge, which is also one of the four evaluation benchmarks, creating a potential optimization-evaluation overlap.
Appendix A.4: official HarmBench classifier and StrongREJECT evaluator used; authors claim PKU-derived attack pools have no exact overlap with the four safety benchmarks (held-out transfer).
Appendix C.2 and C.3: poisoning sweep shows ASR saturating near 20% contamination; a single Refiner→Solver link attack yields 70.0 vs 67.0 for all links, indicating localized vulnerability.
Appendix A.1/A.3: models limited to 1B-8B (Llama-3.2, Qwen2.5/Qwen3, Gemma-3), link sizes 27.3M-111.2M, AdamW lr 5e-4 on a single H100; no seed or variance reporting; no code-release statement found.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly on-topic: safety of LLM multi-agent systems, learned latent communication links as a new attack surface, GRPO-based reward-guided attack/repair, and standard red-team benchmarks (HarmBench, StrongREJECT, JailbreakBench, AdvBench). The core finding—benign link training alone raises aggregate ASR from ~4-12 to ~21-31 with frozen agents (Table 1)—is novel and well-motivated, and the forced-refusal-prefix and first-token analyses (Fig. 2, C.5) give a credible mechanistic account via shallow alignment. Rigor is solid: three topologies, four safety plus two utility benchmarks, poisoning-rate sweep, single-link attack-surface analysis, supervised-vs-RL ablation, and claimed held-out query separation (A.4). Weaknesses: only small open models (1B-8B) and a single benign math training task limit generalizability; no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; the attack reward uses the StrongREJECT judge (B.3) which is also an evaluation benchmark, risking optimistic inflation on that metric; no code release is stated despite detailed hyperparameters and templates. Overall a strong, in-scope safety paper with convincing effect sizes (27.9→76.9 attack; 70.3→4.8 repair) but moderate statistical and scale caveats.

evidence: Section 4.1: on Legal/Nemotron-12B, RoD reduces validation-loss forgetting by 43% vs 10% fixed replay (0.125 to 0.071) and task-based forgetting from 6.7 to 4.9 points at matched adaptation (0.967).

Appendix B.3 'Runs and compute': 'We use seed 42 throughout training and run each experimental condition once. Accordingly, the reported frontiers are single-seed estimates'; conclusions rest on patterns recurring across settings, not repeated runs.

Section 4.3 (Fig. 5a): component ablation shows RHO-based selection within a fixed replay allocation largely maintains the random-selection trade-off; gains emerge only when adaptation and replay compete jointly, isolating the contribution.

Appendix C.3.3 (Fig. 10): vulnerability-to-sampling-ratio correlation r=0.88 for Nemotron-12B German, 0.76/0.66/0.45 elsewhere; Legal-Qwen correlation rises from r=0.20 to r=0.69 after excluding one influential multilingual source.

Section 4.4 / Table 1: curricula built by Qwen3.5-4B remain effective for the 35B target (8.75x gap: adapt 1.751, val. forgetting 0.024 vs no-replay 0.483), and a 4B reference recovers native 9B RoD trade-off.

Appendix C.2 and D.3-D.4: authors acknowledge proxy replay (Nemotron corpus for Qwen) yields weaker coupling between validation-loss and task-based forgetting, with the residual gap concentrated in reasoning/mathematics and multilingual tasks.

Appendix A.1-A.2: derivation of source-specific scores from the RHO objective via three stated approximations; joint top-k optimality shown under a PL-type condition (Eq. 21) and treated as a local marginal-utility surrogate, not a guarantee.

Section 3.3 and Reproducibility statement: implementation on NeMo-RL with code released at https://github.com/bethgelab/replay-on-demand; Algorithm 1, optimizer settings (Adam beta1=0.9, beta2=0.95, lr 1.2e-4), batch 1024x4096, and data preprocessing detailed in Appendix B.

Appendix C.1 (Fig. 6, Table 4): robustness checks showing fixed-replay trained to convergence (up to 2.27x budget) still does not beat RoD's 1x frontier, and RoD does not improve when continued ~20% beyond its budget.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A methodologically relevant LLM-training paper: dynamic replay allocation for continued pretraining via source-specific reducible losses (adaptation scored against a domain specialist, replay against the pretrained model), with joint top-k selection letting the replay share emerge. Strongly matches LLM/training/data-selection preferences; Japanese/agent/safety preferences are not addressed. Novelty is moderate: it composes RHO (Mindermann et al.) with base-relative forgetting signals; the joint allocation rule and its derivation are the main new elements, and the paper honestly positions itself against adaptive-mixture and replay-selection prior work. Rigor is high: 5 model-domain settings across Nemotron/Qwen 4B-35B, fixed-replay sweeps, model-merging, max-replay off-budget reference, component and candidate-multiplier ablations, convergence checks for both RoD and baselines, and a formal derivation with explicitly stated approximations; but every condition is a single seed 42 run, which the authors themselves flag, and several frontier claims are qualitative ('reaches or improves'). Evidence is concrete (Table 3 full frontier numbers, Table 1 cross-scale table, correlation analyses with outlier handling), yet single-run and partly loss-centric. Generalizability is well tested across families, scales (8.75x curriculum transfer) and native vs. proxy replay, with clear limits: needs a representative replay pool and an adaptation reference, and the loss signal decouples from capability retention for proxy replay (reasoning/math gap in Appendix C.2). Reproducibility is strong: Algorithm 1, full hyperparameters, data recipes, evaluation suite, seed, and a public code repository.

Section 2.2/Figure 2C: interaction response retains cross-history nearest-neighbor overlap of 48.06% and 46.50% vs 11.73%/12.08% shuffle control at layer 19, despite occupying only 0.69%/0.66% of displacement energy—supporting a recurring problem-dependent history effect.

Section 4.3/Table 3: shared-T1 AIME 2025 T2 ablations show STAIR 48.33% Avg@4 vs Native 21.67%, Bank-free 36.67%, Random-reflector 37.22%, Direct reflected-read 41.67%, K–V pairing 33.06%; all interventions improve over Native, so the learned differential read over intact K/V pairs is the best but not uniquely beneficial control outcome.

llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM methodology work squarely matching top preferences: LLMs (Qwen3/3.5), attention/transformer internals, mathematical reasoning, and KV-cache/memory for inference. The central question (can computation from completed independent problems aid new ones) is fresh, and the mechanism—learned Householder query reflections producing a differential readout of a frozen historical K/V bank with only 12,288 trainable parameters—is a novel combination of cache-reuse and parameter-efficient ideas beyond Transformer-XL/Memorizing Transformers/Prompt Cache. Rigor is strong: crossed-history replay with additive decomposition, shuffle controls, Bank-free/Random-reflector/Direct-read/K–V-permutation ablations, a LoRA joint-training comparison, and honest reporting of mixed outcomes. Evidence is tempered by small evaluation sets (AIME 30 problems, AMC23† 34), no significance testing, a surprisingly low Native T2 baseline in the shared-T1 study against which all interventions improve, no uniform gains over Vanilla (e.g., Qwen3.5-9B GPQA: STAIR 75.93 vs Native 79.88), and no code release despite exhaustive protocol appendices. Generalizability is limited to four-turn sessions and the Qwen family, as the authors themselves state; out-of-domain transfer to GPQA is inconsistent. Reproducibility is high on paper detail (training settings, scoring rules, exclusion lists, runtime) but lacks an artifact availability claim.

Methodological contribution is solid but incremental over existing post-hoc style/transform watermarking (ACW, SrcMarker, RoSeMary); the genuinely new pieces are style-preference calibration against natural style frequencies (Section 3.1), grade-level aggregation preventing evidence inflation (Section 3.3), and key+context-conditioned target assignment via HMAC-SHA256 for pattern resistance (Section 3.2). llm_evaluation.rationale: A core LLM reasoning / test-time scaling paper that squarely matches high-weight preferences (LLMs, reasoning & CoT, test-time compute, inference). The contribution is a dynamical-systems framing of sequential scaling (states, transitions, attractor definition), systematic quantification of premature convergence to suboptimal attractors across 27 method-model-benchmark combinations, and a simple model-mixing intervention. Novelty is moderate: the paper itself cites roughly ten prior works observing attractor-like convergence in specific settings, and model mixing has known mixed results (Section 2.3); the value lies in unification, compute-matched coverage comparisons, and the negative-result boundary analysis, not a fundamentally new method. Generalizability is reasonable within verifiable maths/game reasoning, with transfer tested to Qwen3 235B, but scope excludes tools, latent/gradient methods, and frontier models. The core conceptual contribution—formalizing Risk-Realization Factors and decoupling the pretext ('why') from an intact actuation ('what') across coordinated skills via persistent artifact preconditioning—is a genuine but incremental twist on a dense line of skill-poisoning work (SkillTrojan/ColluSkill fragment actuation; SkillJect/POISE colocate pretext; SkillHarm/SkillJack already exploit persistent state). Experimental design is unusually careful for an attack paper: steering-only screening isolates ASR to instances where localized attacks fail (Table 1: 76.19% on 128/168 DeepSeek-V4-Flash), ablations quantify each pretext component (Table 3), a trace-summary control rules out context truncation as the driver of the cross-lifecycle 'Fait Accompali'-style effect (Table 8), and payload oracles are deterministic rather than LLM-judged (Appendix C.2). Deductions: uniformly perfect 100% TCR and a uniformly 0.00% Naive baseline are suspiciously clean and under-explained (Naive failing because agents 'fail to observe the Steering Skill' contradicts the qualification step requiring benign steering-skill invocation); no variance, seeds, or significance testing; attack generation/evaluation partially relies on the same GPT-5.5 pipeline model; evaluation confined to a single harness (Claude Code) and SKILL.md threat surface limits generalizability; and the entire model/citation ecosystem (GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, 2026 preprints) is unverifiable. Code release plus detailed prompt templates, contract schemas, and payload provenance (Appendices A–C) support moderate reproducibility, though the named models are not reproducible today. Strong relevance carries the score; rigor and evidence are solid but not airtight.

links.title: PatchKV: Weight-Space Compensation of KV Cache

evidence: Abstract: proposes a training-free framework that 'compensates KV cache compression methods by carrying part of the context in the model's weights' via a context-specific weight patch computed once at context-loading time.
Sec 3.2: 'On SQuAD, in particular, PatchKV recovers up to 73% of full-KV accuracy with no cache, whereas the cache-only baseline collapses to near zero.'

Sec 2.2: patch derivation is 'a gradient-free block-wise ridge regression that patches MLP output projections', explicitly borrowing from Mazzawi et al. [18] and Dherin et al. [4,6] context-to-weight conversion.

Sec 3.3 Table 2: patches built from disjoint 20% cache subsets score best on their source cache (85.39/88.09 diagonal vs 65.63/66.60 off-diagonal), supporting that patches capture compression-lost information.
Sec 3.4 Table 3: chunk-size ablation shows relative accuracy flat at 1K-5K (.696/.695/.696) then dropping at 8K-10K (.672/.679), with memory growing to 35.9GB.
App B.2 Table 5: honest negative result—Attention Matching and Attention Matching+PatchKV both achieve 0.0 on Retr.KV and Retr.Prefix-Suffix at all budgets (0.20-0.01).
App C Table 7: online extension on AIME 2025 uses only 30 problems per cell with mixed outcomes (e.g., 2048→222: AM 2/30 vs AM+PatchKV 8/30 at 4K, but 2048→1034 8K: AM 13/30 vs PatchKV 12/30).

App D Limitations: acknowledges reference-query mismatch risk, one-time preprocessing cost requiring full-cache teacher access, and that multi-context serving of patches 'requires additional serving mechanisms'.
App C Table 6: patch construction costs 153.17s and 32.98GB peak memory for a 169K-token context at budget 0.2, quantifying the one-time overhead claim.

Sec 3.1: evaluation spans three LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B-1M, Qwen3-4B, LLaMA3.1-8B), two compression methods (KVzip, Attention Matching), and benchmarks up to 170K tokens; no code release is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM long-context inference paper (KV cache compression + weight-space compensation), squarely matching LLM, Long Context & Memory, and Inference & Serving preferences. Novelty is moderate: the closed-form ridge activation-matching is adapted from Mazzawi et al. [18] and context-to-weight theory from Dherin et al. [4,6], with Cartridges-style self-study references; the contribution is repurposing these as a compressor-agnostic compensation layer, which is a genuinely new and practical framing versus concurrent KV-side compensation (GRKV, MomentKV). Rigor is solid: three backbones, two compressors, ablations on chunk size, ridge scaling, reference strategies, low-rank patches, precision, plus a clever cross-evaluation of disjoint-cache patches (Table 2) and honest reporting of failure cases (0.0 accuracy on Retr.KV, Table 5). Evidence is decent but headline benchmark results are mostly in figures without exact numbers, and the online AIME extension is tiny (30 problems) with mixed results (12/30 vs 13/30 for AM at 2048→1034, Table 7). Generalizability is strong across models, budgets, quantized caches, and task mixtures. Reproducibility is middling: Algorithm 1 and implementation details are given, but no code release is stated and patch cost (153s, 33GB peak for one context, Table 6) plus context-specific patches limit easy replication. Limitations are candidly discussed in App. D.

evidence: Section 3.2 / Figure 1: frontier models reach ~76% overall accuracy vs 33.3% chance and 66.0% best human on a 50-question subset; Table 4 (Appendix D) shows architecture-only accuracy (e.g., 38% GPT-6 Astra) far below optimizer-only (84-87%).

Section 4, Table 1: zero-shot vs 10-shot comparison shows no reliable ICL gain (e.g., GPT-5.6 Luna 64.0% -> 60.0%), used to support the 'empirical not structured' claim; authors note 50-sample noise threshold of ~7% for test-time scaling tiers.

Section 5 / Figure 7: knowledge base of 20 propositions raises GPT-4o from 53.2% (KB0) to 67.6% (KB8) on a 50-question held-out subset without parameter updates, while Claude Opus 5 fluctuates around its 76% ceiling; selection rule specified in Appendix C.1.

Appendix E, Table 5: strict paired label-flip evaluation (52 accepted pairs) shows combined accuracy 0.462-0.500 and answer-change rates of only 5.8-23.1% when changing the dataset should reverse the correct answer.
Appendix A.3: ground truth requires the winner's worst run across 10 seeds to beat every rival's best run (Eq. 1), with a release audit re-deriving answers and checking leakage for all 500 questions.

Section 6 Discussion: authors concede the benchmark is 'deliberately fully synthetic' with short training horizons and finite family registry, limiting transfer to real-world experiment selection; project URL given as https://github.com/renrua52/ArchitectureIQ.
llm_evaluation.rationale: In-scope LLM research: a benchmark probing whether LLMs can predict neural-network training outcomes before execution, directly engaging high-weight preferences (LLMs, reasoning/CoT, prompting/ICL, evaluation, knowledge transfer). The construction is unusually careful: executable ground truth with a strict 10-seed winner-separation criterion (Appendix A.3), parameter-count control, a release audit, and taxonomy of question types. Findings are quantitatively supported (Table 4: frontier models ~76% vs chance 33.3%; architecture-only weakness down to 38% for GPT-6 Astra) and stress-tested via a clever paired label-flip protocol showing combined accuracy collapses to 0.462-0.500 when the dataset alone flips the winner (Appendix E, Table 5). Novelty is solid but bounded: related ML-agent benchmarks exist, and the contribution is isolation of pre-execution prediction plus a PUCT-style verifiable-proposition knowledge base (Appendix C.1) that lifts GPT-4o from 53.2% to 67.6% (Section 5, Figure 7). Deductions: KB and human evaluations rest on small 50-question subsets; key interpretive claims ('intuition is empirical not structured') rest on null results from noisy small-n ICL (Table 1) and test-time-scaling experiments where the authors admit differences below ~7% are indistinguishable; and the fully synthetic, tiny-scale regime (small MLPs/GRUs, short horizons) limits generalizability to real experiment selection, a limitation the Discussion itself concedes. Reproducibility is supported by a code URL, frozen v1.5 release, and reproduced prompt templates (Appendix B), though the repository is unverified and reported model identifiers are unverifiable. Overall a rigorous, relevant, moderately novel benchmark paper with honest limitations.

Section 4.2 / Table 5: multi-sentence extension (RAMS, CNN/DM, ANLI, LogiQA) shows 'no meaningful improvement from AMR augmentation across all fine-tuning strategies and models', addressing the saturation confound.

Section 5.2 / Table 7: probe result — 'no substantial difference between AMR-augmented perplexity and that of the AMR-nodes control condition', supporting the claim that AMR adds no relational knowledge beyond text.

Section 1: 'We make all code used in these experiments available on GitHub' (footnote 2), plus full prompts and hyperparameters in Appendices A-C, supporting reproducibility; AMR-NLD generation relies on 'Claude Sonnet 4.6' (Section 5.1.1), a partially closed dependency.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A solid, in-scope LLM/NLP methodology paper: a careful reproduction study showing that AMR augmentation does not improve fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B/Qwen3-8B performance, plus a perplexity-based probe (with an AMR-nodes control) explaining why. Preference relevance is strong for LLM fine-tuning/evaluation and NLP tasks, though it touches none of the highest-weight agent/Japanese/reasoning cores beyond incidental task coverage. Novelty is moderate: negative-result reproduction extending Jin et al. (2024) to SFT, with a simple but well-controlled probe as the main new method. Rigor and evidence are high: 5 seeds, grid-searched LRs per configuration, t-tests over 36 configurations, multi-sentence anti-saturation checks, alternative GNN/AMRBART soft-prompt integrations, and an intermediate AMR-to-text objective to rule out format unfamiliarity. llm_evaluation.rationale: Squarely in-scope LLM-agent methodology: iterative self-distillation for agent self-improvement on Qwen3-4B/8B matches high-weight preferences (Agents & Tool Use, LLMs, Training & Optimization, some RL). The contribution is a plug-in (sensitivity-guided step selection via teacher JSD, trajectory loss balancing, privileged-view retention KL) addressing a real, demonstrated failure mode (performance collapse across self-distillation cycles, Figure 1/Table 1 where OEL and SDPO degrade by Cycle 3). Novelty is moderate: each component is a known technique (top-K divergence selection, loss reweighting, teacher-KL regularization); the value is in the diagnosis and combination for the iterative setting. Rigor is above average: six model-benchmark settings, matched budgets, full 2^3 component ablation (Table 2), selection-strategy control (Random/Bottom vs Top, Table 3a), retention-view control (ordinary vs privileged, Table 3b/D.1), hyperparameter sweeps (Table 7), and cost accounting (Table 8). Key limitations: standard deviations capture only decoding variability, not independent training seeds (admitted in Appendix C.1); a single-cycle of three deployments; per-benchmark hyperparameters differ (rho=0.05 vs 0.25, lambda=0.5 vs 1.0); and the AITZ generalization gain is small (65.95% vs 64.89%). Reproducibility is good given full prompt templates, optimizer settings, and infrastructure details, but no explicit code/data release is claimed.

Generalizability is limited by the single model and synthetic SWE-wrapped algorithmic environments, acknowledged in Limitations. Reproducibility is strong: public code release, detailed appendices (SFT composition Table 4, reward equations, full monitor prompt Table 6, rule-based exploit tags Table 7).

Novelty is moderate: logit-level diversity penalties date to Diverse Beam Search and ODD exists for diffusion LMs, but the within-step 'cascade' peer-commitment coupling with information-order asymmetry, the sparsemax allocation result, and the coupling-ceiling bound are genuinely new twists. Calibrated score 0.74 reflects a solid, well-controlled LLM decoding paper with real but incremental contribution.

Sec. 4.1: evaluation uses T=0.6, top-p=0.95, max 65,536 tokens on RTX A6000; no multiple seeds, sampling repetitions, or variance estimates reported anywhere.
Table 1: honest mixed outcomes — Llama-8B AWQ +RATIO ΔAcc +0.06 (negligible) and Qwen-14B AWQ ΔAcc −0.07, so accuracy gains are not uniform across models.

Sec. 4.3 / Table 2: ablations isolate components; TSPD with manual markers is 3.27 points below RATIO accuracy and 49.27% longer CoT under AWQ-W3, but QRBA(λ=1.0) under GPTQ-W3 achieves higher accuracy (38.68 vs 37.40) and shorter CoT (21.91 vs 22.05) than full RATIO, which the authors acknowledge.
Appendix A.1 / Table 3: generalization check on FlatQuant W4A4KV4 (Qwen-1.5B) gives +3.21 avg accuracy and −12.90% CoT, extending beyond weight-only W3.

Appendix B.1–C.3: token sets and normalized penalties (Tables 4–5), QSTI support/stability thresholds (Eqs. 17–28), staged RTV gates (Eqs. 55–61), and logit-correction derivation (Eq. 62–67) are provided; code 'will be available' at github.com/steven-bao1/RATIO (not yet verifiable).
